title: Repair a Broken Ansible Project
story:
A colleague left the bank last month. Their handover note said "the ledger playbook works, just run it". It does not run, it has not run since the handover, and the ledger configuration on both web servers is now whatever it happened to be in March.
Nobody wrote down what is broken. There is more than one thing wrong, and fixing the first one only reveals the next. That is what real handovers look like.
objectives: Diagnose an Ansible failure from the tool's own output rather than by guessing
Use ansible-inventory, --syntax-check, and -v as a deliberate sequence
Recognise the difference between a parse error, a connection error, a template error, and a silent no-op
Restore a project to a state that converges

task.summary: Find and fix everything wrong with the inherited project until it deploys the ledger configuration correctly to both nodes.
task.description:
The project in your workspace is broken in several independent ways. Some failures stop the run immediately; at least one causes no error at all and simply does not do what it looks like it does.
Work outwards from the tools rather than reading the files hopefully:
`ansible-inventory --list` answers "does Ansible understand my inventory, and which hosts and groups does it think exist?" It also parses the variables files, so it fails when one of those is malformed.
`ansible all -m ping` answers "can Ansible actually open a session on these machines?" A host that reports UNREACHABLE has a connection problem, which is a different kind of problem from a task that fails.
`ansible-playbook --syntax-check site.yml` answers "is this a well-formed playbook?" It touches no server, so it is cheap to run after every edit.
`ansible-playbook site.yml` and, when the message is not enough, `ansible-playbook -v site.yml` show what each task actually did and why it stopped.
When you are finished, running the playbook must leave both managed nodes with:
`/etc/jumptotech/app.conf` containing `app_name=ledger`, `app_port=9090`, `app_release=2.4.1`, and a `served_by=` line naming that node.
`/var/log/jumptotech/reload.log` containing `reloaded ledger` — which only appears if the handler genuinely ran.
And it must converge: a second run in a row must report no changes at all. The final check proves this properly. It clears the directories the playbook owns, runs the playbook once and expects it to change things, then runs it again and expects it to change nothing. A playbook that only works on a machine that is already half-configured will not pass it.

requirements: Ansible can parse the inventory and its variables
Both nodes hold a fully rendered configuration
The configuration is rendered per host
The handler ran on both nodes
From a clean node the playbook converges — it changes, then it does not

hints.text: Run the three read-only tools in order before you change anything: `ansible-inventory --list`, then `ansible all -m ping`, then `ansible-playbook --syntax-check site.yml`. Each one tells you about a different layer, and the first one to complain is the one to fix first.

Not every fault produces an error. A play whose `hosts:` pattern matches nothing reports zero hosts and exits successfully; a `notify:` naming a handler that does not exist notifies nothing. Compare what the inventory says the group is called with what the playbook asks for, and compare the handler's name with the string that notifies it — character for character.

Also check the two places a value can silently be the wrong one: the name a variable is defined under versus the name the template asks for, and the filename the template task names versus the file that actually exists. When a run reaches a task and fails inside it, `-v` prints the module's own message, which usually names the argument it did not like.
